FIRETEC Bug Resolution Log May 2026

BUG-2026-05-001: Inconsistent Z-Direction Pressure Gradient
Scaling

File: higrad.F90
Lines: 161-162
Description
The vertical pressure gradients at the bottom (k=1) and top (k=l) boundaries incorrectly include a 0.5
scaling factor, making them half of what they should be.

Code Location

! Lines 161-162 in higrad.F90
pz(i,j,1)= 0.5*(pr(i,j,2)-pr(i,j,1))*dzi
pz(i,j,l)= 0.5*(pr(i,j,l)-pr(i,j,l-1))*dzi

Problem Analysis
These are one-sided finite differences over one grid spacing (dz), so the gradient should be:

• Forward difference at k=1: pz(i,j,1) = (pr(i,j,2)-pr(i,j,1))*dzi
• Backward difference at k=l: pz(i,j,l) = (pr(i,j,l)-pr(i,j,l-1))*dzi

The 0.5 factor is incorrect because:

• Interior points (k=2 to l-1) use centered differences with 2*dz spacing, so 0.5 factor is correct there
  (line 154)
• Boundary points use 1*dz spacing, so no 0.5 factor should be applied
• This is inconsistent with how x and y boundaries are handled (lines 118, 124, 139, 146) where 0.5 is
  correctly omitted

Impact
• Vertical pressure forces are underestimated by 50% at top and bottom
• Creates artificial vertical pressure imbalance
• Contributes to vertical wave reflections at boundaries
• With uniform dz=1, these errors accumulate faster
• Compounds with other boundary errors to create instabilities

Comparison with Correct X/Y Boundary Treatment
X-direction boundaries (lines 118, 124):

px(1,j,k)=(pr(2,j,k)-pr(1,j,k))*dxi      ! Correct - no 0.5 factor
px(np,j,k)=(pr(np,j,k)-pr(np-1,j,k))*dxi ! Correct - no 0.5 factor

Z-direction boundaries (lines 161-162):

 8

FIRETEC Bug Resolution Log May 2026

pz(i,j,1)= 0.5*(pr(i,j,2)-pr(i,j,1))*dzi   ! WRONG - has 0.5 factor
pz(i,j,l)= 0.5*(pr(i,j,l)-pr(i,j,l-1))*dzi ! WRONG - has 0.5 factor

Recommended Fix
Remove the 0.5 scaling factor:

do j=1,mp
  do i=1,np
    pz(i,j,1) = (pr(i,j,2)-pr(i,j,1))*dzi
    pz(i,j,l) = (pr(i,j,l)-pr(i,j,l-1))*dzi
  enddo
enddo

Git evidence: 8093f01 (2026-05-21, higrad pressure-gradient endpoint update).
The pressure-initialization code was changed in CODE-dev/higrad.F90 so the bottom and top vertical
pressure-gradient endpoints use one-sided second-order finite differences rather than the earlier incon-
sistent endpoint scaling.

BUG-2026-05-002: Boundary Updates in MOA Time Extrapolation

File: MOA.F90
Lines: 68-77
Description
Time-extrapolated velocities in the MOA inner loop are not properly updated at boundaries before
being used in advection calculations, leading to uninitialized ghost cell values.

Code Location

! Lines 68-70: Time extrapolation (interior points only)
u(i,j,k,2)=0.5*(3.*u(i,j,k,1)-u(i,j,k,0))
v(i,j,k,2)=0.5*(3.*v(i,j,k,1)-v(i,j,k,0))
o(i,j,k,2)=0.5*(3.*o(i,j,k,1)-o(i,j,k,0))

! Lines 76-77: These extrapolated arrays are passed with ghost cells
call setAdvectiveVelocities(u(:,:,:,2),v(:,:,:,2),o(:,:,:,2), &
  1-ih,np+ih,1-ih,mp+ih,l,dts,0)

Problem Analysis
1. The time extrapolation loop only covers interior cells (i=1,np, j=1,mp, k=1,l)
2. Ghost cells (i.e., i<1, i>np, j<1, j>mp) in the time level "2" arrays remain uninitialized
3. These uninitialized arrays are passed to setAdvectiveVelocities
4. Inside setAdvectiveVelocities (advectionScheme.F90, lines 121, 161), update() is called:

   call update(u,u,np,mp,l,1-ih,np+ih,1-ih,mp+ih,2,0)
   call update(v,v,np,mp,l,1-ih,np+ih,1-ih,mp+ih,3,0)

5. The update() routine fills ghost cells with environmental values (ae) for boundary processors
6. However, at ymax (topdedge==1), the ghost cells are filled with:

 a(i,nyp+j,k)=ae(iref,nyp,k) ! update.F90 line 356

 This uses the uninitialized ghost cell values from the extrapolated field

Impact at ymax Boundary
• Ghost cells at j>mp contain garbage/uninitialized values from time extrapolation
• These get used in subsequent advection flux calculations
• Errors propagate into the physical domain through the advection scheme
• With uniform dz=1, vertical advection is more active, amplifying these errors
• Compounds with aggressive relaxation to create explosive growth

Call Chain Showing the Problem

MOA.F90:
  u(:,:,:,2) extrapolated -> ghost cells UNINITIALIZED

 11

FIRETEC Bug Resolution Log May 2026

 =>
 setAdvectiveVelocities() -> uses uninitialized ghost cells
 =>
 update() -> fills ghost cells but uses uninitialized base values
 =>
 Advection calculations -> use bad ghost cell values
 =>
 Errors propagate into physical domain

Recommended Fix
Add proper boundary updates immediately after time extrapolation:

! After lines 68-70, add:
call update(u(:,:,:,2),u(:,:,:,2),np,mp,l,1-ih,np+ih,1-ih,mp+ih,2,0)
call update(v(:,:,:,2),v(:,:,:,2),np,mp,l,1-ih,np+ih,1-ih,mp+ih,3,0)
call update(o(:,:,:,2),o(:,:,:,2),np,mp,l,1-ih,np+ih,1-ih,mp+ih,0,0)

! Then proceed with:
call setAdvectiveVelocities(u(:,:,:,2),v(:,:,:,2),o(:,:,:,2), &
  1-ih,np+ih,1-ih,mp+ih,l,dts,0)

Git evidence: ee83e79 (2026-06-09, zeta bug-list pass); 0792741 (2026-06-15, mirrored-boundary corner
rewrite); fd65110 (2026-08-11, metric/MOA fixes and fuel limits).
The exact suggested immediate u/v/o halo update was not preserved as a standalone patch. The landed
implementation rewrote the update interface and boundary flags, removed the unused ae argument,
and later bundled MOA-related cleanup with the fuel-limit fixes.

BUG-2026-05-003: Heat-source behavior controls were global instead
of per-source

Files: variables_heat.F90, input_heat.F90, heatsource_heat.F90

The old module had scalar control variables such as isource_function, imass_source, and MLRHRRin-
puts. In a multi-source run, every source therefore had to use the same source-function waveform, the
same mass-source option, and the same MLR/HRR input mode.

The code looped over itsource but read and used scalar configuration. That made nsource_hs only
partially useful: geometric arrays were per-source, but important behavior switches were shared across
all sources.

Multi-source cases could not model sources with different waveforms, different mass-source methods, or
only selected sources using time-series MLR/HRR input. A source that should have been constant
could unintentionally inherit a pulsating or file-driven behavior intended for another source.

Git evidence: 94a3ace (2026-06-04, comprehensive heat-source fixes); fa39917 (2026-06-04, multiple
heat sources and end-time support).
The heat-source input path was converted from mostly global controls to per-source arrays, including
multiple heat sources and independent endtime_hs handling. Activation reporting was also added so the
runtime announces source timing more clearly.

BUG-2026-05-004: Heat sources did not have independent start and
end times

Files: variables_heat.F90, input_heat.F90, heatsource_heat.F90

The previous heating routine only checked a scalar starttime_hs in the gridlist module and had no
end-time gate. The fuel-burning update routine did not check time at all, so rhof could be reduced
inside a source footprint even before activation or after deactivation.

Time activation was not stored in the HeatSource variables as per-source state, and updateHeatSource-
Position did not import the simulation time or any heat-source timing arrays.

Sources could remain active forever after their start time and fuel could be consumed outside the
intended active interval. Multi-source activation schedules were not representable.

Git evidence: 94a3ace (2026-06-04, comprehensive heat-source fixes); fa39917 (2026-06-04, multiple
heat sources and end-time support).
The heat-source input path was converted from mostly global controls to per-source arrays, including
multiple heat sources and independent endtime_hs handling. Activation reporting was also added so the
runtime announces source timing more clearly.

FIRETEC Bug Resolution Log May 2026

BUG-2026-05-005: XY coverage was based on point tests rather than
actual cell/source overlap

Files: heatsource_heat.F90

Circular and rectangular sources were selected using different point conventions: sometimes ia*dx,
sometimes ia*dx + dx/2, and rectangular heating required the whole cell to fit inside the rectangle.
Partial cells on source boundaries were either ignored or treated as fully covered.

The old code tested a single point or full-cell bounds rather than the intersection of the source footprint
with each grid cell. For circular sources, a cell near the circle edge could be incorrectly included or
excluded depending on where its center or corner fell.

Boundary cells could cause grid-resolution-dependent source area, heat release, and fuel burn. Rectan-
gular sources could shrink when a rectangle edge cut through cells. Circular sources could be jagged
and inconsistent between fuel burn and heating.

Git evidence: 94a3ace (2026-06-04, comprehensive heat-source fixes); 2a0e05f (2026-06-04, small
heat-source fix); fa39917 (2026-06-04, multiple heat sources and end-time support).
The heat-source geometry routines were revised so source forcing is distributed over the covered cells
and depth interval rather than relying only on point-in-box tests. The follow-up commit tightened
smaller edge cases in that implementation.

FIRETEC Bug Resolution Log May 2026

BUG-2026-05-006: Depth handling ignored terrain height and partial
vertical-cell coverage

Files: heatsource_heat.F90

The old depth check used zcart(zedge(k),i,j) < depth_hs(itsource). That compares absolute vertical
coordinate to source depth and only tests the lower cell face. A cell crossing the source top was counted
fully, and terrain elevation zs was not subtracted.

The code treated depth as an absolute z limit instead of depth above local ground/surface. It also did
not compute the fraction of a vertical cell inside the source depth.

On terrain-following or non-flat grids, a source depth intended to mean meters above ground could be
applied at the wrong elevation. Cells that only partly intersected the heat-source depth could receive a
full forcing contribution.

Git evidence: 94a3ace (2026-06-04, comprehensive heat-source fixes); 2a0e05f (2026-06-04, small
heat-source fix); fa39917 (2026-06-04, multiple heat sources and end-time support).
The heat-source geometry routines were revised so source forcing is distributed over the covered cells
and depth interval rather than relying only on point-in-box tests. The follow-up commit tightened
smaller edge cases in that implementation.

FIRETEC Bug Resolution Log May 2026

BUG-2026-05-007: MLR/HRR input reading was fragile and not
truly per-source

Files: rinit_heat.F90, variables_heat.F90, heatsource_heat.F90

The previous rinitHeatSource used a single MLRHRRinputs flag, opened/read files for all sources
when that scalar was enabled, and used restart logic based on repeated backspace calls. Runtime
advancement read at most one record per call and did not preserve an EOF state.

Restart scanning and normal advancement assumed the file pointer and time-step cadence would
cooperate. If a restart time was before the first record, after the last record, or if a step skipped over
multiple records, the old logic could select the wrong bracket or fail to clamp cleanly. Read errors were
not consistently distinguished from EOF.

File-driven sources could use stale HRR/MLR values, fail on restart, or continue trying to read after
EOF. Sources not intended to use MLR/HRR input were also tied to a global file-input choice.

Git evidence: 61944bc (2026-06-08, MLR/HRR input fix); 94a3ace (2026-06-04, comprehensive heat-
source fixes); fa39917 (2026-06-04, multiple heat sources and end-time support); ba0bb93 (2026-07-23,
heat-source HRR/MLR initial value fix).
The MLR/HRR input and interpolation path was repaired for multiple sources. A later July follow-up
also clamps times before the first tabulated value to the first MLR/HRR entry instead of extrapolating
backward from it.

BUG-2026-05-008: HRR and MLR file values were distributed
incorrectly across source cells

Files: heatsource_heat.F90

When MLR/HRR input was enabled, the old code computed energy as HRR/cell_volume inside every
selected cell. That applies the total HRR independently to each selected cell rather than distributing
the total HRR over the whole source volume. The mass-source option had the same pattern when
fm_hs was added cell-by-cell.

The old code had no source_volume calculation. In parallel, no global reduction was performed, so a
correct total source volume was not available across MPI ranks.

Total injected heat and mass could scale with the number of selected cells or the decomposition, rather
than matching the intended MLR/HRR time-series value. Boundary cells were also not weighted by
fractional coverage.

Git evidence: 61944bc (2026-06-08, MLR/HRR input fix); 94a3ace (2026-06-04, comprehensive heat-
source fixes); fa39917 (2026-06-04, multiple heat sources and end-time support); ba0bb93 (2026-07-23,
heat-source HRR/MLR initial value fix).
The MLR/HRR input and interpolation path was repaired for multiple sources. A later July follow-up
also clamps times before the first tabulated value to the first MLR/HRR entry instead of extrapolating
backward from it.

FIRETEC Bug Resolution Log May 2026

BUG-2026-05-009: Interpolation and zero-time tolerance checks
could divide by zero or use the wrong denominator

Files: heatsource_heat.F90

The old interpolation guard checked abs((TME(1)-TME(2))/TME(1)) < tolerance. If TME(1) was
zero, this could divide by zero. The check also measured relative difference against the first timestamp
rather than directly checking whether the two bracketing timestamps were effectively identical.

Time-series files commonly begin at time zero. A zero first timestamp is valid input, so using it as a
denominator is unsafe.

At best, this produced fragile floating-point behavior; at worst, it could trigger a divide-by-zero or
choose the wrong interpolation path.

Git evidence: 61944bc (2026-06-08, MLR/HRR input fix); 94a3ace (2026-06-04, comprehensive heat-
source fixes); fa39917 (2026-06-04, multiple heat sources and end-time support); ba0bb93 (2026-07-23,
heat-source HRR/MLR initial value fix).
The MLR/HRR input and interpolation path was repaired for multiple sources. A later July follow-up
also clamps times before the first tabulated value to the first MLR/HRR entry instead of extrapolating
backward from it.

BUG-2026-05-010: Input documentation did not describe
multi-source constraints or new array inputs

Files: input_heat.F90

The original input routine contained no embedded instructions for the new multi-source array semantics.
After moving settings to arrays, users need to know that all sources in a run share the same geometry
type selected by iheatsource, while individual parameter arrays are indexed by source.

Without documentation near the parser, it would be easy to supply mixed circular/rectangular inputs
or scalar legacy keys that no longer control individual sources.

Misconfigured inputs could appear to run but apply the wrong shape, timing, source function, or
MLR/HRR behavior to one or more sources.

Git evidence: 7861033 (2026-06-04, heat-source instructions); fa39917 (2026-06-04, multiple heat
sources and end-time support).
The input documentation was updated with the new heat-source controls and the implementation now
expects the expanded per-source timing and configuration arrays.

June 2026

Overview

This note summarizes likely bugs and suspicious patterns found in the velocity transport path across
the Fortran source files.
The main recurring theme is that x-direction and y-direction velocity boundary behavior appears to
be swapped in several routines. In particular, u/x-direction quantities are being treated as normal
to top/bottom boundaries, while v/y-direction quantities are being treated as normal to left/right
boundaries. This appears reversed for conventional Cartesian velocity components.

 38

FIRETEC Bug Resolution Log June 2026

BUG-2026-06-001: Symmetric/mirror velocity boundary flags are
reversed across multiple routines

Known or likely affected files include:

• advectionScheme.F90
 – mpdata
 – setAdvectiveVelocities
• MOA.F90
• force.F90
 – large-step force advection
• domainUpdates.F90
 – explicit_domain_updates
 – implicit_domain_updates
 – xvrho halo updates
• rinit.F90
 – rinit
 – setVelocityProfile
• update.F90
 – misleading explanatory comment
• likely related turbulent-domain variants as well

Summary
For symmetric or mirror boundary conditions, the code appears to reverse the normal-velocity parity
flags for the horizontal velocity components.
The update() routine uses the arguments topbot and leftright to decide whether a variable should be
odd-reflected, meaning sign-reversed, at a boundary.
The meaning appears to be:

topbot = 1 -> odd reflection at bottom/top j-boundaries
leftright = 1 -> odd reflection at left/right i-boundaries

For conventional Cartesian velocity components:

u / iuvel -> x-direction velocity or x-momentum
v / ivvel -> y-direction velocity or y-momentum

Therefore the expected mirror/symmetric parity is:

u is normal to left/right boundaries -> leftright = 1
v is normal to bottom/top boundaries -> topbot = 1

However, many call sites use the opposite mapping:

 39

if(kv.eq.1) then
  topbot = 1
  leftright = 0
elseif(kv.eq.2) then
  topbot = 0
  leftright = 1
else
  topbot = 0
  leftright = 0
endif

Given that xvpointers defines:

iuvel = 1
ivvel = 2
iwvel = 3

this means:

u is being odd-reflected at top/bottom instead of left/right.
v is being odd-reflected at left/right instead of top/bottom.

Why this is likely wrong
The advection setup treats:

u -> x-direction face velocity / x-face flux
v -> y-direction face velocity / y-face flux

For example, in setAdvectiveVelocities(), u is used to form u1 with dxi, while v is used to form u2 with
dyi.
That strongly indicates:

u / u1 / f1 -> x-direction, normal to left/right boundaries
v / u2 / f2 -> y-direction, normal to bottom/top boundaries

The current parity logic is therefore reversed.

This affects symmetric or mirror boundaries, especially cases where one or more of the following are
set to mirror/symmetric behavior:

ibc_top
ibc_bot
ibc_left
ibc_right

wrong wall-normal velocity behavior,
spurious normal fluxes near physical boundaries,

 40

incorrect tangential velocity reflection,
boundary-generated numerical artifacts,
incorrect behavior near symmetric/mirror boundaries,
bad velocity ghost cells in xv or xvrho,
downstream corruption in turbulence, drag, firebrand, and convection-related calculations.

At left/right boundaries:

u, the normal component, is incorrectly even-reflected.
v, the tangential component, is incorrectly odd-reflected.

At bottom/top boundaries:

v, the normal component, is incorrectly even-reflected.
u, the tangential component, is incorrectly odd-reflected.

Because the transported variables may be momentum-like quantities, for example rho*u and rho*v,
the same parity logic still applies: the normal momentum component should be odd-reflected, while
tangential momentum and scalar fields should be even-reflected.

Replace repeated hard-coded logic such as:

if(kv.eq.1) then
  topbot = 1
  leftright = 0
elseif(kv.eq.2) then
  topbot = 0
  leftright = 1
else
  topbot = 0
  leftright = 0
endif

with pointer-based logic:

topbot = 0
leftright = 0

if(kv.eq.iuvel) then
  leftright = 1
elseif(kv.eq.ivvel) then
  topbot = 1
endif

Make sure each affected routine has access to the symbolic velocity indices, for example:

use xvall, only : iuvel, ivvel

or add iuvel and ivvel to the existing use xvall, only : ... list.
A cleaner long-term fix would be to centralize this in a helper routine:

 41

subroutine symmetric_bc_flags(kv,topbot,leftright)
  use xvall, only : iuvel, ivvel
  implicit none

  integer,intent(in) :: kv
  integer,intent(out) :: topbot, leftright

  topbot = 0
  leftright = 0

  if(kv.eq.iuvel) then
 leftright = 1
  elseif(kv.eq.ivvel) then
 topbot = 1
  endif
end subroutine symmetric_bc_flags

Then callers can use:

call symmetric_bc_flags(kv,topbot,leftright)

Additional hard-coded cases in setAdvectiveVelocities
setAdvectiveVelocities() contains hard-coded update() calls that appear to use the same reversed
convention.
Current pattern:

call update(u,u,np,mp,l,1-ih,np+ih,1-ih,mp+ih,2,0,1,0)
call update(v,v,np,mp,l,1-ih,np+ih,1-ih,mp+ih,3,0,0,1)

Since u is the x-direction component, it should be odd at left/right boundaries, not top/bottom. Since
v is the y-direction component, it should be odd at top/bottom boundaries, not left/right.
These should likely be:

call update(u,u,np,mp,l,1-ih,np+ih,1-ih,mp+ih,2,0,0,1)
call update(v,v,np,mp,l,1-ih,np+ih,1-ih,mp+ih,3,0,1,0)

Face-centered advective velocity updates also appear reversed.
Current pattern:

call update(u1,u1,np+1,mp,l,1-ih,np+ih+1,1-ih,mp+ih,1,1,1,0)
call update(u2,u2,np,mp+1,l,1-ih,np+ih,1-ih,mp+ih+1,1,2,0,1)

Since u1 is the x-face advective velocity, it should be odd at left/right boundaries. Since u2 is the y-face
advective velocity, it should be odd at top/bottom boundaries.
These should likely be:

call update(u1,u1,np+1,mp,l,1-ih,np+ih+1,1-ih,mp+ih,1,1,0,1)
call update(u2,u2,np,mp+1,l,1-ih,np+ih,1-ih,mp+ih+1,1,2,1,0)

 42

Other hard-coded update() calls for x-face and y-face flux-like arrays in mpdata() should also be audited.
Keep the explicit audit list searchable, including:

u, v
u1, u2, u3
f1, f2, f3
v1mp, v2mp, v3mp

The large-step force-advection path in force.F90 should also be searched explicitly for forceLE_xv, because
it appears to use the same hard-coded kv.eq.1 / kv.eq.2 boundary-flag convention before donor-cell
advection.
The xvrho halo-update path should be treated as a first-class affected case, not just a downstream
consequence. Bad xvrho ghost cells can propagate into turbulence, drag, firebrand, and convection-
related calculations even if the main transported xv array is corrected elsewhere.
General rule:

x-direction face quantities -> topbot = 0, leftright = 1
y-direction face quantities -> topbot = 1, leftright = 0

This applies when the quantity being updated represents a normal velocity or flux component for
mirror boundary-condition purposes.

Comment fix in update.F90
The explanatory comment in update.F90 appears to have the velocity directions reversed.
The comment says that u is normal to the top and bottom of the domain and that v has the opposite
settings. Given the code indexing and velocity pointers, this should be corrected to say:

u is normal to left/right boundaries.
v is normal to bottom/top boundaries.

update() itself appears internally consistent. The bug is primarily in callers that assign the flags
backwards, plus the misleading comment.

Git evidence: ee83e79 (2026-06-09, zeta bug-list pass); 4343edc (2026-06-10, top/bottom mirror-
boundary fix); 0792741 (2026-06-15, mirrored-boundary corner rewrite).
The boundary flag plumbing was rewritten around loop_update_flags and the mirror-boundary top/bot-
tom swap was fixed explicitly. A later corner rewrite removed the old ae argument and reduced
duplicated edge-condition branches.

FIRETEC Bug Resolution Log June 2026

BUG-2026-06-002: MPDATA assumes density is the last transported
variable instead of using irho

File
• advectionScheme.F90

Summary
The MPDATA limiter and density correction logic appear to assume that the density variable is always
the final transported variable, nvp.
For example:

a(i,j,k,kv) = x(i,j,k,kv) / x(i,j,k,nvp)

The code also treats:

f1(...,nvp)
f2(...,nvp)
f3(...,nvp)

as density fluxes.
However, elsewhere the code uses an explicit density pointer:

irho

This means MPDATA silently assumes:

irho == nvp

or, at the call site:

irho == nv

Additional related issue
The density correction coefficients are initialized only when kv.eq.1:

if (kv.eq.1) cpmp(i,j,k,nvp)=tmpp
if (kv.eq.1) cnmp(i,j,k,nvp)=tmpn

Then density limiter coefficients are minimized over all:

kv = 1,nvp-1

This assumes:

density is variable nvp,
all variables before density should constrain the density anti-diffusive correction.

 46

That may be intentional for a particular MPDATA/FCT formulation, but it is fragile and tightly
coupled to variable ordering.

If density is not the final transported variable, the limiter may compute ratios using the wrong
denominator. This can corrupt:

velocity transport,
scalar transport,
density correction,
limiter behavior,
boundedness.

Pass irho explicitly into mpdata():

subroutine mpdata(x,h,xe,il,iu,jl,ju,lls,nvp,irho)

Then replace density references to nvp with irho where appropriate.
For example:

a(i,j,k,kv) = x(i,j,k,kv) / x(i,j,k,irho)

Replace loops such as:

do kv = 1,nvp-1

with logic that loops over all transported variables except irho.
At minimum, add a defensive check:

if (irho .ne. nvp) stop ’mpdata␣assumes␣irho␣==␣nvp’

Also add comments explaining whether density anti-diffusive correction should be constrained by
velocity and scalar extrema.

Git evidence: 0325b25 (2026-07-14, MPDATA cleanup); ee83e79 (2026-06-09, zeta bug-list pass).
MPDATA was cleaned up and its update calls were moved to the newer boundary-flag interface. I did
not find a literal refactor replacing every last-variable density use with irho; the current limiter still
relies on the transported density slot convention in several expressions.

BUG-2026-06-003: tinit side relaxation/damper boundary setup
uses inconsistent boundary indexing

File
• tinit.F90

Summary
The side relaxation/damper setup in tinit appears to have two related indexing problems:

1. Boundary coordinate checks appear swapped between x and y directions.
2. relb is populated by boundary number but later accessed by boundary-condition type.

Together, these can apply damping or relaxation to the wrong physical side of the domain or with the
wrong profile.

3.1 Boundary coordinate checks appear swapped
The code labels boundaries as top, bottom, left, and right, but appears to check the opposite coordinate
direction.
Assuming:

i = x index
j = y index
n = global x extent
m = global y extent
ia = global x index
ja = global y index

the expected mapping is:

top boundary -> ymax -> ja.gt.m-nr
bottom boundary -> ymin -> ja.le.nr
left boundary -> xmin -> ia.le.nr
right boundary -> xmax -> ia.gt.n-nr

The current mapping appears to be:

bcs(1), top -> checks xmax
bcs(2), bottom -> checks xmin
bcs(3), left -> checks ymin
bcs(4), right -> checks ymax

This can apply relaxation or damping on the wrong physical sides of the domain.

spurious relaxation near xmin when bottom damping was intended,

 50

spurious relaxation near ymin when left damping was intended,
a weird line at xmin,
another artifact near ymin,
missing or weakened relaxation near intended top/bottom/left/right sides,
artificial source-like behavior in the first few cells of the wrong coordinate direction,
long boundary-aligned artifacts unrelated to the intended physical boundary condition.

Suggested correction
The logic should be closer to:

ia = (npos-1)*np + i
ja = (mpos-1)*mp + j

! top boundary: ymax
if(bcs(1).ge.1.and.bcs(1).lt.5) then
  if(ja.gt.m-nr) then
 do it=1,4
 relaxxv(i,j,k,it)=max(relaxxv(i,j,k,it), relb(1,m-ja+1))
 enddo
  endif
endif

! bottom boundary: ymin
if(bcs(2).ge.1.and.bcs(2).lt.5) then
  if(ja.le.nr) then
 do it=1,4
 relaxxv(i,j,k,it)=max(relaxxv(i,j,k,it), relb(2,ja))
 enddo
  endif
endif

! left boundary: xmin
if(bcs(3).ge.1.and.bcs(3).lt.5) then
  if(ia.le.nr) then
 do it=1,4
 relaxxv(i,j,k,it)=max(relaxxv(i,j,k,it), relb(3,ia))
 enddo
  endif
endif

! right boundary: xmax
if(bcs(4).ge.1.and.bcs(4).lt.5) then
  if(ia.gt.n-nr) then
 do it=1,4
 relaxxv(i,j,k,it)=max(relaxxv(i,j,k,it), relb(4,n-ia+1))
 enddo
  endif
endif

3.2 relb appears indexed by boundary-condition type instead of boundary number
relb is allocated with the first index representing the boundary number:

allocate(relb(4,nr+1))

 51

It is populated using j, where j = 1..4 corresponds to the physical boundary:

do j=1,4
  if(bcs(j).ge.1.and.bcs(j).lt.5) then
 select case(bcs(j))
 case(4)
         relb(j,i)=...
 case(3)
         relb(j,i)=...
 case(2)
         relb(j,i)=...
 case(1)
         relb(j,i)=...

  endif
enddo

So:

relb(1,:) -> profile for boundary 1
relb(2,:) -> profile for boundary 2
relb(3,:) -> profile for boundary 3
relb(4,:) -> profile for boundary 4

However, later the code appears to access relb using the boundary-condition type as the first index:

relb(bcs(1), ...)
relb(bcs(2), ...)
relb(bcs(3), ...)
relb(bcs(4), ...)

If bcs(1)=3, this reads from relb(3,:) instead of relb(1,:).

This can apply the wrong relaxation strength or profile to a boundary. In some configurations, it
may read from a row that was not populated for that boundary, producing missing, zero, or incorrect
relaxation.

Index relb by boundary number, not by boundary-condition type.
Replace accesses like:

relb(bcs(1), ...)
relb(bcs(2), ...)
relb(bcs(3), ...)
relb(bcs(4), ...)

with:

relb(1, ...)
relb(2, ...)
relb(3, ...)
relb(4, ...)

 52

Enable only one boundary relaxation/damper at a time and confirm that nonzero relaxxv appears only
near the corresponding physical side.
Example checks:

enable only bcs(1) / top
expected nonzero relaxxv only near ymax

enable only bcs(2) / bottom
expected nonzero relaxxv only near ymin

enable only bcs(3) / left
expected nonzero relaxxv only near xmin

enable only bcs(4) / right
expected nonzero relaxxv only near xmax

This should be checked in global coordinates using:

ia = (npos-1)*np + i
ja = (mpos-1)*mp + j

so the test also covers decomposed-domain behavior.

3.3 relaxxv may be used before being explicitly initialized
relaxxv is imported from xvall and then assigned selectively in the vertical absorber and side-damper
logic. However, the routine does not explicitly zero relaxxv before using it in expressions such as:

relaxxv(i,j,k,it)=max(relaxxv(i,j,k,it),relb(...))

This is unsafe unless relaxxv is guaranteed to have been initialized elsewhere before every call to tinit.
The max() pattern is especially risky because an uninitialized or stale value can survive and become the
final relaxation coefficient.

Why this matters
The relaxation coefficient is later applied directly as a tendency in boundary.F90:

force(i,j,k,kv)=force(i,j,k,kv)+relaxxv(i,j,k,min(kv,4))* &
  (xe(i,j,k,kv)-xv(i,j,k,kv))/dt

Therefore any garbage, stale, or unintended nonzero value in relaxxv becomes a direct forcing term.
This is a strong candidate for spurious velocities at or near relaxation boundaries.

Explicitly initialize the full relaxation array at the start of tinit, before any vertical or side-damper
assignments:

relaxxv = 0.0_prec

 53

If relaxxv is allocatable and may not be allocated yet, place the initialization immediately after its
allocation point instead, or add a defensive allocation/initialization check in the owning module.

Before applying the relaxation force, print or assert the min/max of relaxxv for each component and
verify that nonzero values appear only in intended damping/relaxation regions.
Example diagnostic:

write(*,*) ’relaxxv␣min/max␣comp␣1:’, minval(relaxxv(:,:,:,1)), maxval(relaxxv(:,:,:,1))
write(*,*) ’relaxxv␣min/max␣comp␣2:’, minval(relaxxv(:,:,:,2)), maxval(relaxxv(:,:,:,2))
write(*,*) ’relaxxv␣min/max␣comp␣3:’, minval(relaxxv(:,:,:,3)), maxval(relaxxv(:,:,:,3))
write(*,*) ’relaxxv␣min/max␣comp␣4:’, minval(relaxxv(:,:,:,4)), maxval(relaxxv(:,:,:,4))

3.4 The first two side-relaxation cells are forced to coefficient 1.0
After constructing the side relaxation profiles, tinit overrides the first two cells for every boundary
profile:

relb(:,1:2)=1. ! Mass conservation and Neumann boundary conditions

This creates a hard two-cell relaxation layer, independent of the smoother profile selected by the
boundary-condition type.

Because boundary.F90 applies relaxation as:

force = force + relaxxv * (xe - xv) / dt

using relaxxv = 1 means the affected variable is driven toward the environmental state over one timestep,
assuming the time integrator later multiplies the tendency by dt. That is effectively a hard local reset,
not a gradual sponge layer.
Such a discontinuity in relaxation strength can generate sharp momentum, pressure, density, or scalar
gradients adjacent to the relaxation region. This can plausibly create spurious velocities near the
relaxation BCs even if the side and profile indexing bugs are fixed.

Suggested fix or test
Do not hard-set the first two cells to 1.0 unless that behavior is required by the numerical method and
has been verified not to create artifacts.
A minimal diagnostic test is to comment out the override:

! relb(:,1:2)=1.

or replace it with a capped value:

 54

relb(:,1:2) = min(relb(:,1:2), 0.1_prec)

A cleaner approach is to incorporate any special near-boundary behavior into the selected relaxation
profile so that the coefficient varies smoothly.

Run a case with only one side relaxation boundary enabled and compare velocity magnitude near the
first several relaxation cells with:

relb(:,1:2)=1.

enabled versus disabled or capped. If the artifact collapses when the hard reset is removed, this is a
direct contributor.

3.5 Top theta-relaxation profile likely uses the wrong vertical offset
The iab.eq.4 theta relaxation branch uses zabt in the activation condition and denominator, but uses
zab in the numerator:

if(iab.eq.4.and.zl.ge.zabt) &
  relaxxv(i,j,k,4)=0.66*0.25*(1.-cos(pi*(zl-zab)/(zb-zabt)))/tow

This appears inconsistent. If theta relaxation starts at zabt, the profile argument should likely also
start from zabt.

If zab and zabt differ, the theta-relaxation profile may be discontinuous at the activation height or
may start with an unintended nonzero value. It could also become negative or otherwise mis-scaled
depending on the relative values of zab, zabt, and zb.
This is less directly tied to side relaxation BC artifacts than the relaxxv initialization and relb issues,
but it can still produce unintended vertical forcing in potential temperature near the top absorber.

Use a consistent offset for the theta absorber:

if(iab.eq.4.and.zl.ge.zabt) &
  relaxxv(i,j,k,4)=0.66*0.25*(1.-cos(pi*(zl-zabt)/(zb-zabt)))/tow

Also guard against zb == zabt.

 55

3.6 Side relaxation and top absorber share relaxxv, so lateral boundary mistakes
can appear inside the top relaxation domain
File
• tinit.F90
• Related application path:
 – boundary.F90
 – small_implicit_forcings in force.F90

Summary
The vertical/top absorber and the lateral side relaxation/damper appear to write into the same
relaxation coefficient array:

relaxxv(i,j,k,it)

The side-damper logic appears to merge its coefficients with whatever is already present in relaxxv
using a pattern like:

relaxxv(i,j,k,it)=max(relaxxv(i,j,k,it),relb(...))

This means relaxxv is not purely a top-absorber mask or purely a side-relaxation mask. It is a combined
relaxation mask used later as a direct forcing coefficient.
That is fine if both masks are built correctly. However, if the lateral side-relaxation indexing is wrong,
or if relb is indexed incorrectly, then side-boundary damping can be merged into regions that visually
appear to belong to the top relaxation domain.
This is a plausible explanation for artifacts where y-boundary behavior appears reflected, projected, or
painted into the upper/top relaxation layer.

boundary.F90 applies relaxxv directly as a tendency:

force(i,j,k,kv)=force(i,j,k,kv)+relaxxv(i,j,k,min(kv,4))* &
  (xe(i,j,k,kv)-xv(i,j,k,kv))/dt

Therefore, any unintended nonzero value in relaxxv becomes an actual relaxation force.
Since the side-damper construction uses max() rather than assignment, a bad lateral mask can survive
and combine with the vertical absorber instead of being overwritten. This makes the final relaxation
field harder to interpret: an artifact visible in the top absorber may actually originate from the
side-relaxation setup.
This issue is closely related to the earlier tinit concerns:

3.1 boundary coordinate checks appear swapped
3.2 relb appears indexed by boundary-condition type instead of boundary number
3.3 relaxxv may be used before being explicitly initialized
3.4 hard two-cell relb(:,1:2)=1.0 side-relaxation region
3.5 top theta-relaxation vertical-profile issue

 56

The key additional point here is that these effects may be visually or diagnostically misattributed to
the top absorber because side relaxation and top relaxation are stored in the same array.

y-boundary relaxation pattern appearing in the top relaxation domain,
top absorber showing horizontal structure that should only belong to side boundaries,
apparent reflection of bottom/top lateral boundary behavior into the upper domain,
relaxation forcing applied in unintended regions,
spurious velocity, theta, density, or scalar forcing near the upper sponge layer,
confusing diagnostics where the artifact appears vertical/top-related but is caused by lateral mask
 ,→ construction,
sensitivity to which side boundary condition is enabled,
sensitivity to bcs(1:4) values and to nr.

This is especially suspicious if:

the top absorber should be horizontally uniform,
but relaxxv varies in x or y inside the top absorber,
or enabling/disabling a y-side boundary changes the relaxation pattern near the top.

Suggested diagnostic
Output or inspect relaxxv immediately after tinit, before time stepping begins and before boundary.F90
applies it.
At minimum, print component min/max values:

write(*,*) ’relaxxv␣min/max␣comp␣1:’, &
  minval(relaxxv(:,:,:,1)), maxval(relaxxv(:,:,:,1))
write(*,*) ’relaxxv␣min/max␣comp␣2:’, &
  minval(relaxxv(:,:,:,2)), maxval(relaxxv(:,:,:,2))
write(*,*) ’relaxxv␣min/max␣comp␣3:’, &
  minval(relaxxv(:,:,:,3)), maxval(relaxxv(:,:,:,3))
write(*,*) ’relaxxv␣min/max␣comp␣4:’, &
  minval(relaxxv(:,:,:,4)), maxval(relaxxv(:,:,:,4))

More useful diagnostics are horizontal slices of relaxxv:

near the bottom of the top absorber,
inside the middle of the top absorber,
near the top of the top absorber,
near each lateral side boundary,
and outside all intended relaxation regions.

Recommended test matrix:

1. top absorber only, all side relaxation disabled
2. top/ymax side relaxation only
3. bottom/ymin side relaxation only
4. left/xmin side relaxation only
5. right/xmax side relaxation only
6. top absorber plus one side relaxation at a time

 57

Expected behavior:

top absorber:
  relaxxv should vary primarily with vertical position and should not inherit side-boundary-shaped
 ,→ horizontal patterns unless intentionally designed.

top/ymax side relaxation:
  nonzero lateral relaxxv should occur only near ja > m - nr.

bottom/ymin side relaxation:
  nonzero lateral relaxxv should occur only near ja <= nr.

left/xmin side relaxation:
  nonzero lateral relaxxv should occur only near ia <= nr.

right/xmax side relaxation:
  nonzero lateral relaxxv should occur only near ia > n - nr.

Use global indices when checking decomposed-domain behavior:

ia = (npos-1)*np + i
ja = (mpos-1)*mp + j

Suspicious behavior:

enabling a y-side boundary changes relaxxv in an x-side region,
enabling a y-side boundary creates structure inside the top absorber,
top absorber relaxxv has a lateral side-damper footprint,
relaxxv remains nonzero outside intended vertical or lateral relaxation zones,
relaxxv changes depending on bcs values in a way that follows boundary-condition type rather than
 ,→ physical boundary number.

Suggested fix or hardening
The best fix is to make the vertical/top relaxation and lateral side relaxation construction explicit and
separately diagnosable.
A minimal hardening approach is:

relaxxv = 0.0_prec

before any top or side relaxation coefficients are assigned.
Then, if possible, build separate temporary arrays:

relax_top(:,:,:,:)
relax_side(:,:,:,:)

or at least separate diagnostic fields, and combine only after both masks are known to be correct:

relaxxv = max(relax_top, relax_side)

This would make it much easier to determine whether an artifact originates in the vertical absorber or
the lateral side damper.

 58

If separate arrays are too invasive, add temporary diagnostics around the two construction phases:

! after vertical/top absorber construction
write(*,*) ’after␣top␣absorber␣relaxxv␣min/max:’, minval(relaxxv), maxval(relaxxv)

! after side relaxation construction
write(*,*) ’after␣side␣relaxation␣relaxxv␣min/max:’, minval(relaxxv), maxval(relaxxv)

Also fix or verify the side-relaxation indexing issues from Sections 3.1 and 3.2 before interpreting the
merged relaxxv field.
The side-relaxation mapping should be checked against:

top boundary -> ymax -> ja > m - nr
bottom boundary -> ymin -> ja <= nr
left boundary -> xmin -> ia <= nr
right boundary -> xmax -> ia > n - nr

and relb should be indexed by physical boundary number:

relb(1,...)
relb(2,...)
relb(3,...)
relb(4,...)

not by boundary-condition type:

relb(bcs(1),...)
relb(bcs(2),...)
relb(bcs(3),...)
relb(bcs(4),...)

After implementing the above diagnostics or fixes, verify that:

1. With side relaxation disabled, the top absorber is horizontally smooth/uniform as expected.
2. With top absorber disabled, each side relaxation appears only on its intended physical side.
3. With both enabled, the merged relaxxv field equals the expected max/top-plus-side combination.
4. No y-boundary-shaped structure appears in the top absorber unless it is physically intended.
5. The relaxation forcing in boundary.F90 is nonzero only where the final relaxxv mask is
 ,→ intentionally nonzero.

If the observed top-domain artifact disappears when side relaxation is disabled, or if it follows a single
enabled side boundary, then the root cause is likely in the side-relaxation mask construction rather
than in the vertical top absorber itself.
This issue may not be a separate root bug from Sections 3.1 through 3.3, but it explains how those
bugs can present as a top-relaxation-domain artifact. It should be treated as the main diagnostic link
between the observed y-boundary reflection and the tinit side-relaxation indexing problems.

Git evidence: ee83e79 (2026-06-09, zeta bug-list pass); 4233690 (2026-06-15, tinit indexing fix).

 59

The side-relaxation indexing in CODE-dev/tinit.F90 was corrected to use the appropriate global/local
edge indexing, and the follow-up commit fixed a remaining processor-boundary indexing issue.

BUG-2026-06-004: ibcx / ibcy boundary-condition remapping
appears swapped

File
• Input/grid boundary-condition handling code

Summary
The boundary-condition remapping appears to assign ibcx to top/bottom boundaries and ibcy to
left/right boundaries:

if(ibc_top.eq.7825) ibc_top = ibcx
if(ibc_bot.eq.7825) ibc_bot = ibcx
if(ibc_left.eq.7825) ibc_left = ibcy
if(ibc_right.eq.7825) ibc_right = ibcy

If ibcx is intended to control x-direction boundaries, it should apply to left/right boundaries. Likewise,
ibcy should apply to bottom/top boundaries.

The current mapping could cause the x-domain or y-domain to appear cyclic or non-cyclic incorrectly,
depending on the gridlist values being used.
This may be connected to observed weird cycling of the x-domain when non-periodic boundary
conditions are set.

Swap the mapping so that ibcx controls left/right boundaries and ibcy controls bottom/top boundaries:

if(ibc_left.eq.7825) ibc_left = ibcx
if(ibc_right.eq.7825) ibc_right = ibcx
if(ibc_bot.eq.7825) ibc_bot = ibcy
if(ibc_top.eq.7825) ibc_top = ibcy

Git evidence: ee83e79 (2026-06-09, zeta bug-list pass).
The input remapping was corrected so default left/right settings map to the x-boundary array and
top/bottom settings map to the y-boundary array.

BUG-2026-06-005: Non-periodic x-boundaries still communicate with
periodic x-neighbors

• msga.F90
• update.F90
 – update
• advectionScheme.F90
 – setAdvectiveVelocities
 – related MPDATA face-flux updates
• related halo-update call sites that rely on peleft and peright
• related x-face or x-flux arrays:
 – u1
 – f1
 – v1mp
 – other arrays with local x extent np+1

Summary
The MPI setup identifies physical left/right domain edges using leftedge and rightedge, but the
x-direction neighbor ranks still appear to be assigned with wraparound behavior.
The relevant logic is equivalent to:

peleft = mpi_rank - 1
if (peleft < ((mpos-1)*nprocx)) peleft = mpi_rank + (nprocx-1)

peright = mpi_rank + 1
if (peright > (mpos*nprocx-1)) peright = mpi_rank - (nprocx-1)

This means that a rank on the global left x-edge still treats the global right x-edge rank as its left
neighbor, and a rank on the global right x-edge still treats the global left x-edge rank as its right
neighbor.
Later, update.F90 performs x-direction halo exchanges whenever icorner.ne.3:

call MPI_Sendrecv(... peleft ... peright ...)
call MPI_Sendrecv(... peright ... peleft ...)

Only after the MPI exchange does update() overwrite physical ghost cells for non-periodic boundaries.
A focused subcase is the iperiod=1 path for x-face arrays with local extent np+1; at a non-periodic xmax,
a(np+1) is a physical boundary face, not a periodic duplicate of the neighbor's a(1), so u1 and related
x-face flux arrays should be explicitly checked.

For a non-periodic x-domain, ranks on physical left/right edges should not exchange halo data across
the global x-boundary. Physical ghost cells at those edges should be filled only by non-periodic
boundary-condition logic.

 64

The current behavior makes the MPI topology periodic even when the boundary condition is non-
periodic.
The later ghost-cell overwrite may hide the issue for ordinary cell-centered arrays, but the communication
itself is still inconsistent with the requested boundary condition. It also assumes every array passed
through update() has a complete and correct physical-boundary repair step after the exchange. That
assumption is fragile for face-flux arrays, corner-update paths, and future update paths.

This can produce apparent x-domain cycling in non-periodic runs.

apparent wraparound or cycling of x-domain data despite non-periodic boundary settings,
stale or invalid edge data entering halo buffers,
boundary artifacts near global left/right edges,
inconsistent behavior between fields that are corrected after update() and fields that are not,
fragile behavior for face-flux arrays or corner-update paths,
spurious xmax artifacts,
apparent wraparound of x-face velocities or x-fluxes,
bad antidiffusive velocities near the right physical boundary,
incorrect x-face fluxes in MPDATA near xmax,
boundary-aligned numerical noise near i=np or i=np+1,
sensitivity to processor decomposition in x.

The most suspicious arrays to inspect are:

u1
f1
v1mp

and any other x-face or x-flux arrays with effective x extent np+1.

Do not wrap x-neighbor ranks across physical non-periodic boundaries.
A minimal fix is to set physical-edge x-neighbors to MPI_PROC_NULL after computing leftedge, rightedge,
peleft, and peright:

if (leftedge.eq.1) then
  peleft = MPI_PROC_NULL
endif

if (rightedge.eq.1) then
  peright = MPI_PROC_NULL
endif

If diagonal or corner neighbor ranks are also wrapped periodically, they should be handled consistently.
Any neighbor relationship that crosses a physical non-periodic x-boundary should either be set to
MPI_PROC_NULL or skipped in the corresponding communication path.

 65

More robust fix
Make update() locally safe by guarding the x-direction exchange against physical non-periodic edges,
even if the global neighbor setup changes elsewhere.
For example:

xleft_neighbor = peleft
xright_neighbor = peright

if (leftedge.eq.1) then
  xleft_neighbor = MPI_PROC_NULL
endif

if (rightedge.eq.1) then
  xright_neighbor = MPI_PROC_NULL
endif

Then use xleft_neighbor and xright_neighbor in the x-direction MPI_Sendrecv calls instead of using peleft
and peright directly.
For face-centered arrays, also add defensive checks or comments clarifying that:

a(np+1,j,k) is a physical xmax face on rightedge ranks when x is non-periodic.
a(np+2:np+ih+1,j,k) are right ghost faces and must be filled from physical boundary logic, not
 ,→ periodic wraparound.

A safer long-term design would be to make update() aware of whether the domain direction is actually
periodic, instead of relying only on iperiod, which currently describes array indexing periodicity rather
than physical boundary periodicity.

Additional hardening
Some face-flux arrays appear to be passed through update() before their physical boundary flux values
are filled. For example, in advectionScheme.F90, the left-edge flux construction can skip f1(1,j,k,kv) on
a left-edge rank, call update(f1,...), and only afterward fill the physical boundary value.
That ordering is fragile.
A safer pattern is:

! Fill physical boundary fluxes before halo update
if (leftedge.eq.1) then
  f1(1,j,k,kv) = donor(...)
endif

call update(f1(...), ...)

This is secondary to fixing the periodic MPI neighbor mapping, but it reduces the chance that stale or
invalid physical-boundary data enters halo communication.

Git evidence: ee83e79 (2026-06-09, zeta bug-list pass); 0792741 (2026-06-15, mirrored-boundary corner
rewrite); 869ead7 (2026-06-25, boundary-error pass).

 66

The halo-update path was reworked so physical side boundaries and periodic/cyclic exchanges are
selected through explicit per-direction flags rather than always communicating with periodic neighbors.

BUG-2026-06-006: Face-centered iperiod=1 handling for np+1 x-face
arrays at non-periodic xmax

• update.F90
 – update
• advectionScheme.F90
 – setAdvectiveVelocities
 – related MPDATA face-flux updates
• Related arrays:
 – u1
 – f1
 – v1mp
 – other x-face or x-flux arrays with local x extent np+1

Summary
The update() routine has special iperiod logic for face-centered arrays whose local x-size is np+1.
The comment in update.F90 explains that iperiod=1 was introduced for arrays defined on x-faces:

! For arrays defined on cell face dim [1-ih, np+1+ih],
! il=1-ih,iu=np+1+ih, nxp=np+1 and i0=1
...
! because a(np+1) of current proc is equal to a(1) of peright and
! a(1) of current proc to a(np+1) of peleft. (period is np and not
! np+1)

That reasoning is valid for periodic x-face arrays. However, at a non-periodic physical xmax boundary,
the face

a(np+1,j,k)

is not a periodic duplicate of the neighbor's a(1,j,k). It is the physical right boundary face.
Therefore, for x-face arrays on a rank with:

rightedge.eq.1

and non-cyclic ibc_right, a(np+1,j,k) should be treated as a physical boundary face. It should not be
treated as an interior-equivalent periodic face or as a copy of the global xmin side.

setAdvectiveVelocities() updates the x-face advective velocity u1 using:

call update(u1,u1,np+1,mp,l,1-ih,np+ih+1,1-ih,mp+ih,1,1,1,0)

Here:

 69

nxp = np+1
iperiod = 1

Inside update(), iperiod=1 sets:

i0 = 1

The x-direction MPI exchange then fills right ghost faces as:

a(nxp+i,j,k)

which, for nxp=np+1, means:

a(np+2:np+ih+1,j,k)

At a physical right boundary, the later right-edge boundary fill repairs those ghost cells with:

a(nxp+i,j,k)=ae(nxp,jref,k)

so for nxp=np+1:

a(np+2:np+ih+1,j,k) = ae(np+1,jref,k)

This means update() does not obviously overwrite a(np+1,j,k) itself in the physical-edge repair section.
The physical boundary face appears to remain intact.
However, the broader Issue 5 problem still applies: before physical-edge repair, the MPI exchange can
still communicate with a wrapped periodic neighbor because peright and peleft are assigned periodically.
Thus, for np+1 face arrays, the right ghost faces may first receive values from the global xmin side and
only later be overwritten by the physical boundary repair.
This ordering is fragile. It assumes that:

1. all non-periodic physical ghost cells are fully repaired after communication,
2. no code reads the temporary periodic ghost values before repair,
3. all face-centered arrays use correct nxp, iperiod, and edge-fill conventions,
4. corner and face-flux update paths are also fully repaired.

That assumption should be explicitly tested for np+1 x-face arrays.

Important nuance
This is not yet proven to be a direct overwrite of:

a(np+1,j,k)

For the standard right-edge fill, update() writes:

a(np+2:np+ih+1,j,k)

not:

 70

a(np+1,j,k)

So the suspected failure mode is not necessarily:

a(np+1) is overwritten by periodic data

but rather:

x-face ghost cells beyond np+1 may temporarily or incorrectly contain periodic wrapped data,
and some face-flux or antidiffusive-velocity path may use that data before or instead of the physical
 ,→ boundary repair.

This should be treated as a focused subcase of Issue 5, not as a completely separate confirmed bug.

If the iperiod=1, np+1 face-array path leaks periodic neighbor data at a non-periodic xmax, possible
symptoms include:

spurious xmax artifacts,
apparent wraparound of x-face velocities or x-fluxes,
bad antidiffusive velocities near the right physical boundary,
incorrect x-face fluxes in MPDATA near xmax,
boundary-aligned numerical noise near i=np or i=np+1,
sensitivity to processor decomposition in x.

The most suspicious arrays to inspect are:

u1
f1
v1mp

and any other x-face or x-flux arrays with effective x extent np+1.

Recommended diagnostic
On a rank with:

rightedge.eq.1

and non-periodic ibc_right, print or check the physical boundary face and right ghost faces before and
after update().
For u1, around this call in setAdvectiveVelocities():

call update(u1,u1,np+1,mp,l,1-ih,np+ih+1,1-ih,mp+ih,1,1,1,0)

check:

u1(np+1,j,k)
u1(np+2:np+ih+1,j,k)

 71

before and after the call.
Expected behavior:

u1(np+1,j,k) should remain the physical xmax face value.
u1(np+2:np+ih+1,j,k) should be filled from the physical boundary face,
usually copied or sign-reflected from u1(np+1,jref,k), depending on the BC.

Suspicious behavior:

u1(np+1,j,k) changes during update().
u1(np+2:np+ih+1,j,k) matches values from global xmin.
u1(np+2:np+ih+1,j,k) matches another rank’s a(1,j,k) rather than local a(np+1,j,k).
right ghost values differ before/after only because of periodic exchange and are read by later code
 ,→ before repair.

A minimal debug pattern is:

if(rightedge.eq.1) then
  write(*,*) ’BEFORE␣update␣u1␣rank/rightedge:’, &
    ’␣u1(np+1)=’, u1(np+1,j,k), &
    ’␣u1(np+2)=’, u1(np+2,j,k)
endif

call update(u1,u1,np+1,mp,l,1-ih,np+ih+1,1-ih,mp+ih,1,1,1,0)

if(rightedge.eq.1) then
  write(*,*) ’AFTER␣update␣u1␣rank/rightedge:’, &
    ’␣u1(np+1)=’, u1(np+1,j,k), &
    ’␣u1(np+2)=’, u1(np+2,j,k)
endif

For broader coverage, use a fixed j,k, or loop over representative values:

j = max(1,mp/2)
k = max(1,l/2)

and also inspect near corners:

j = 1
j = mp

because corner repair and side repair may interact.

Related MPDATA arrays
The MPDATA arrays f1 and v1mp are also x-face or x-flux-like arrays with np+1 behavior. Their update
calls should be audited separately because they do not always use iperiod=1; some paths pass nxp=np+1
with iperiod=0.
Examples to search for:

call update(f1(...), ...)
call update(v1mp(...), ...)

 72

especially calls where the x upper bound is:

np+ih+1

or where the effective nxp is conditionally changed from np to np+1 on rightedge.
Even if these paths are not literally iperiod=1, they are part of the same face-centered boundary-risk
class because they carry x-face flux information near xmax.

Suggested fix or hardening
The primary fix remains the broader Issue 5 fix: do not communicate across non-periodic physical
x-boundaries.
For example, use MPI_PROC_NULL or skip x-direction send/recv at physical non-periodic x-edges:

xleft_neighbor = peleft
xright_neighbor = peright

if(leftedge.eq.1) xleft_neighbor = MPI_PROC_NULL
if(rightedge.eq.1) xright_neighbor = MPI_PROC_NULL

and use those local neighbor variables in the x-direction MPI_Sendrecv calls.
For face-centered arrays, also add defensive checks or comments clarifying that:

a(np+1,j,k) is a physical xmax face on rightedge ranks when x is non-periodic.
a(np+2:np+ih+1,j,k) are right ghost faces and must be filled from physical boundary logic, not
 ,→ periodic wraparound.

A safer long-term design would be to make update() aware of whether the domain direction is actually
periodic, instead of relying only on iperiod, which currently describes array indexing periodicity rather
than physical boundary periodicity.

Run a small decomposed case with:

nprocx > 1
rightedge = 1 on the xmax rank
ibc_right > 0
ibc_left > 0

and initialize an easily recognizable non-periodic pattern, for example:

global xmin values = 1000 + local pattern
global xmax values = 2000 + local pattern

Then verify after update() that xmax ghost cells for u1 and related x-face arrays do not contain the xmin
pattern.
Useful checks:

u1(np+1,j,k) ! physical boundary face
u1(np+2:np+ih+1,j,k) ! right ghost faces

 73

f1(np+1,j,k,kv)
f1(np+2:np+ih+1,j,k,kv)

v1mp(np+1,j,k,kv)
v1mp(np+2:np+ih+1,j,k,kv)

If np+2:np+ih+1 contains global-xmin-like values after the final update() return, this is a confirmed bug.
If those values only appear transiently inside update() before physical repair, then the main risk is
ordering fragility and should be fixed by removing non-periodic wraparound communication.

BUG-2026-06-007: Turbulence stress routine has likely sign errors in
z-face y-gradients

File
• stressrij_turb.F90

Summary
In the z-face stress calculation, the y-gradient terms appear to use + where a central-difference stencil
should use -.
Current pattern:

uy = 0.5*(xvrho(i,j+1,kk,iuvel)-xvrho(i,j-1,kk,iuvel)+ &
  xvrho(i,j+1,k-1,iuvel)+xvrho(i,j-1,k-1,iuvel))*hdyi

The same pattern appears for vy and wy.

Why this is likely wrong
Analogous x-face and y-face gradient code uses difference terms at both adjacent planes. The z-face
version should likely average two y-derivatives, not add one value from j+1 and one value from j-1.

Use minus signs in the second plane contribution:

uy = 0.5*(xvrho(i,j+1,kk,iuvel)-xvrho(i,j-1,kk,iuvel)+ &
  xvrho(i,j+1,k-1,iuvel)-xvrho(i,j-1,k-1,iuvel))*hdyi

vy = 0.5*(xvrho(i,j+1,kk,ivvel)-xvrho(i,j-1,kk,ivvel)+ &
  xvrho(i,j+1,k-1,ivvel)-xvrho(i,j-1,k-1,ivvel))*hdyi

wy = 0.5*(xvrho(i,j+1,kk,iwvel)-xvrho(i,j-1,kk,iwvel)+ &
  xvrho(i,j+1,k-1,iwvel)-xvrho(i,j-1,k-1,iwvel))*hdyi

This affects velocity transport indirectly through turbulent momentum forcing.

Git evidence: 1d6c99f (2026-06-09, stressrij scheme fixes); ee83e79 (2026-06-09, zeta bug-list pass).
The turbulence stress routine was patched in CODE-dev/subGridTurb/stressrij_turb.F90 to correct the
z-face y-gradient signs identified in the report.

BUG-2026-06-008: MPI status variable has the wrong type in update

File
• update.F90

Summary
In update, the MPI status variable is declared as part of a real allocatable array list:

real(prec),allocatable :: tmpxsnd(:),tmpxrcv(:),tmpysnd(:), &
  tmpyrcv(:),tmpcorsnd(:),tmpcorrcv(:),sndrcvStatus(:)

However, MPI status objects should be integer arrays, not real arrays.

Passing a real array where MPI expects a status object is undefined behavior.
Depending on compiler and MPI implementation, this can produce memory corruption or other
hard-to-diagnose runtime behavior.
This may not be the most direct cause of boundary-line artifacts, but it is a real correctness issue.

Remove sndrcvStatus from the real allocatable declaration and either declare it correctly:

real(prec),allocatable :: tmpxsnd(:),tmpxrcv(:),tmpysnd(:), &

integer :: sndrcvStatus(MPI_STATUS_SIZE)

or, if the status is not used, replace the status argument in the relevant MPI call with:

MPI_STATUS_IGNORE

Use MPI_STATUS_IGNORE if returned status values are not needed later.

Git evidence: 7c10434 (2026-06-11, integer MPI status initialization); ee83e79 (2026-06-09, zeta bug-list
pass).
The MPI status storage in CODE-dev/update.F90 was changed to an integer status array and initialized
with the integer literal 0.

BUG-2026-06-011: update() physical edge halo fill order lets
left/right boundaries overwrite corner ghost cells

File
• update.F90
 – update

Summary
At physical domain boundaries, update() fills the top and bottom edge halos first, then fills the right
and left edge halos afterward. The top/bottom loops cover the full halo-extended x range:

if(topedge.eq.1)then
  do k=1,nzp
 do j=1,ih
 do i=1-ih,nxp+ih
 ...
        a(i,nyp+j,k)=...
 enddo
 enddo
  enddo
endif

if(botedge.eq.1)then
  do k=1,nzp
 do j=1,ih
 do i=1-ih,nxp+ih
 ...
        a(i,1-j,k)=...
 enddo
 enddo
  enddo
endif

Later, the right/left loops cover the full halo-extended y range:

  do k=1,nzp
 do j=1-ih,nyp+ih
 do i=1,ih
 ...
        a(nxp+i,j,k)=...
 enddo
 enddo
  enddo
endif

  do k=1,nzp
 do j=1-ih,nyp+ih
 do i=1,ih
 ...
        a(1-i,j,k)=...
 enddo
 enddo

 85

  enddo
endif

Because the top/bottom loops include:

i = 1-ih : nxp+ih

and the left/right loops include:

j = 1-ih : nyp+ih

both sets of logic write the physical corner ghost cells. The final corner value is therefore determined
by the later right/left boundary fill, not by a combined or explicitly defined corner boundary condition.
For example, on a top-right physical corner, topedge first writes:

a(nxp+i,nyp+j,k) = ...

but rightedge later overwrites the same cells:

a(nxp+i,nyp+j,k) = ...

For simple copy or Neumann-style boundary conditions, the two writes often produce the same value,
so the issue can remain hidden.
However, for symmetric or mirror boundary conditions, the sign depends on the topbot and leftright
flags. The top-edge symmetric rule can apply one sign convention:

if (ibc_top.eq.5) then
  iref=max(1,min(i,nxp))
  if(topbot.eq.1) a(i,nyp+j,k)=-ae(iref,nyp,k)
  if(topbot.eq.0) a(i,nyp+j,k)= ae(iref,nyp,k)
endif

while the later right-edge logic can apply a different rule:

if (ibc_right.eq.5) then
  jref=max(1,min(j,nyp))
  if(leftright.eq.1) a(nxp+i,j,k)=-ae(nxp,jref,k)
  if(leftright.eq.0) a(nxp+i,j,k)= ae(nxp,jref,k)
endif

Thus a corner ghost cell may be written once according to the top/bottom symmetric rule and then
overwritten according to the right/left symmetric rule. The final corner ghost value depends on
implementation order rather than on an explicitly defined corner condition.

This can produce inconsistent corner ghost cells when one or more of the following are true:

 86

ibc_top, ibc_bot, ibc_left, or ibc_right use symmetric BCs, i.e. ibc_* = 5
different variables use different topbot / leftright mirror flags
the boundary condition type differs between adjacent physical edges
a stencil reads diagonal/corner halo cells
the affected feature originates near a physical corner, especially near xmax/rightedge

For an artifact near xmax, the most relevant regions to inspect are:

i = np+1:np+ih
j = 1-ih:0

and:

i = np+1:np+ih
j = mp+1:mp+ih

These should be compared against the pure right-side halo strip:

i = np+1:np+ih
j = 1:mp

If the artifact starts at an xmax corner and then propagates into the domain, this overwrite order is a
plausible source.
This may be harmless for ordinary copy-style boundary conditions, but it is a real latent bug for mixed
or mirror/symmetric boundary conditions.

Avoid defining corner ghost cells implicitly through overlapping edge loops.
One option is to restrict the right/left physical edge fills to the non-corner j range:

do j=1,nyp

instead of:

do j=1-ih,nyp+ih

and similarly restrict top/bottom fills to the non-corner i range:

do i=1,nxp

instead of using the halo-extended x range. Then fill the four physical corner halo blocks explicitly
afterward.
For symmetric or mirror boundary conditions, the corner sign should be determined by the combination
of the two relevant boundary reflections. Conceptually:

sgn = 1.0_prec

if(top corner .and. ibc_top.eq.5 .and. topbot.eq.1) &
  sgn = -sgn

 87

if(bot corner .and. ibc_bot.eq.5 .and. topbot.eq.1) &
  sgn = -sgn

if(right corner .and. ibc_right.eq.5 .and. leftright.eq.1) &
  sgn = -sgn

if(left corner .and. ibc_left.eq.5 .and. leftright.eq.1) &
  sgn = -sgn

a(corner ghost) = sgn * ae(nearest interior corner)

That makes the corner behavior explicit and independent of fill order.
If the intended behavior is instead that right/left boundaries always dominate at physical corners,
that should be documented clearly. Otherwise, the current behavior is order-dependent and likely
unintended.

Git evidence: ee83e79 (2026-06-09, zeta bug-list pass); 0792741 (2026-06-15, mirrored-boundary corner
rewrite).
The physical-edge halo fill in CODE-dev/update.F90 was reorganized to separate side faces from corner
cells, preventing left/right handling from clobbering corner ghost values.

BUG-2026-06-012: metric.F90 forces c13/c23 to zero at physical side
boundaries, creating possible terrain-metric discontinuities

• metric.F90
 – metric
• Related:
 – topo.F90
 ∗ topo
 – MOA.F90
 ∗ MOA
 – advectionScheme.F90
 ∗ gradmoa
 – domainUpdates.F90
 ∗ explicit_domain_updates
 – subGridTurb/turbFieldUpdate.F90
 ∗ turbFieldUpdate

Summary
metric() computes the terrain-following horizontal/vertical coupling metrics c13 and c23 from go, where:

go(i,j)=zb/(zb-zs(i,j))

The interior c13 metric is computed with a centered difference:

do j=1,mp
  do i=1+leftedge,np-rightedge
    c13(i,j)=.5*(1./go(i+1,j)-1./go(i-1,j))*go(i,j)/dx
  enddo
enddo

but at physical left/right boundaries it is hard-set to zero:

  do j=1,mp
    c13(1,j)=0.
  enddo
endif

  do j=1,mp
    c13(np,j)=0.
  enddo
endif

Similarly, c23 is computed with a centered difference in the interior:

 91

FIRETEC Bug Resolution Log June 2026

do i=1,np
  do j=1+botedge,mp-topedge
    c23(i,j)=.5*(1./go(i,j+1)-1./go(i,j-1))*go(i,j)/dy
  enddo
enddo

but at physical bottom/top boundaries it is hard-set to zero:

if(botedge.eq.1)then
  do i=1,np
    c23(i,1)=0.
  enddo
endif

if(topedge.eq.1)then
  do i=1,np
    c23(i,mp)=0.
  enddo
endif

This means that at physical side boundaries:

c13(1,:) = 0
c13(np,:) = 0
c23(:,1) = 0
c23(:,mp) = 0

regardless of the actual one-sided topographic slope implied by zs.
The related topo() routine also enforces zero-normal-gradient topography at physical boundaries:

if(leftedge.eq.1) then
  do j=1-ih,mp+ih
 zs(1,j)=zs(2,j) !zero gradient
 do i=1,ih
      zs(1-i,j)=zs(1,j)
 enddo
  enddo
endif

if(rightedge.eq.1) then
  do j=1-ih,mp+ih
 zs(np,j)=zs(np-1,j) !zero gradient
 do i=1,ih
      zs(np+i,j)=zs(np,j)
 enddo
  enddo
endif

if(botedge.eq.1) then
  do i=1-ih,np+ih
    zs(i,1)=zs(i,2)
 do j=1,ih
      zs(i,1-j)=zs(i,1)
 enddo
  enddo
endif

 92

if(topedge.eq.1) then
  do i=1-ih,np+ih
    zs(i,mp)=zs(i,mp-1)
 do j=1,ih
      zs(i,mp+j)=zs(i,mp)
 enddo
  enddo
endif

So the zeroed metric is consistent with the current imposed zero-normal-slope terrain boundary
condition. However, if the input topography has nonzero slope as it approaches a physical boundary,
the code silently modifies the edge terrain and then forces the corresponding metric to zero. This can
create a sharp metric kink near the physical boundary.

c13 and c23 are not passive diagnostics. They directly enter several dynamical operators.
In gradmoa(), they modify the pressure-gradient force:

g13=c13(i,j)*gmul(k)
g23=c23(i,j)*gmul(k)
g33= gi(i,j,k)

forceSI_xv(i,j,k,iuvel)=forceSI_xv(i,j,k,iuvel) &
  -(px(i,j,k)+g13*pz(i,j,k))

forceSI_xv(i,j,k,ivvel)=forceSI_xv(i,j,k,ivvel) &
  -(py(i,j,k)+g23*pz(i,j,k))

forceSI_xv(i,j,k,iwvel)=forceSI_xv(i,j,k,iwvel) &
  -(g33*pz(i,j,k))

In MOA, they affect the contravariant vertical velocity:

o(i,j,:,1)=(xv(i,j,:,iwvel)*gi(i,j,:) &
  +c13(i,j)*gmul(:)*xv(i,j,:,iuvel) &
  +c23(i,j)*gmul(:)*xv(i,j,:,ivvel))/xv(i,j,:,irho)/gi(i,j,:)

and later:

o(i,j,k,1)=(xvtmp(i,j,k,iwvel)*gi(i,j,k) &
  +c13(i,j)*gmul(k)*xvtmp(i,j,k,iuvel) &
  +c23(i,j)*gmul(k)*xvtmp(i,j,k,ivvel))/xvtmp(i,j,k,irho) &
  /gi(i,j,k)

They also enter bottom/subground boundary treatment in explicit_domain_updates():

g13 = c13(i,j)*gmul(1)
g23 = c23(i,j)*gmul(1)
g33 = g13**2+g23**2+gi(i,j,1)**2

and turbulence metric terms in turbFieldUpdate():

 93

J31 = c13(i,j)*gmul(k)
J32 = c23(i,j)*gmul(k)

sqrtG_KG33(i,j,k) = sqrtG_Kxy(i,j,k) * (J31**2+J32**2) &
  +sqrtG_Kz(i,j,k) * gi(i,j,k)**2

Therefore, a discontinuity in c13 or c23 is a discontinuity in the modeled coordinate transformation
and in the horizontal/vertical coupling used by pressure, advection, bottom boundary conditions, and
turbulence.
For example, if the terrain approaches the right boundary with a nonzero x-slope, the interior c13(np-1,j)
may be nonzero, but the boundary value is forced to:

c13(np,j)=0.

This creates an abrupt transition:

c13(np-2,j) ~= terrain slope metric
c13(np-1,j) ~= terrain slope metric
c13(np,j)      = 0

The analogous issue exists for:

left boundary: c13(1,j)
right boundary: c13(np,j)
bottom boundary: c23(i,1)
top boundary: c23(i,mp)

This may be intentional if the model requires terrain to become exactly zero-normal-slope at physical
side boundaries. But if the input topography is not already tapered to zero slope, the code creates an
artificial metric transition at the boundary.

This can produce boundary-aligned artifacts when one or more of the following are true:

physical, non-cyclic side boundaries are used
input topography has nonzero normal slope near a physical boundary
terrain is steep near xmin/xmax/ymin/ymax
pressure-gradient forcing is active over sloped terrain
vertical velocity / contravariant velocity coupling is important
subgrid turbulence or bottom boundary treatment reads c13/c23 near edges
the affected feature originates near a physical boundary and propagates inward

Most suspicious regions are:

left physical boundary:
i = 1
j = 1:mp
c13(1,:)

right physical boundary:
i = np
j = 1:mp
c13(np,:)

 94

bottom physical boundary:
i = 1:np
j = 1
c23(:,1)

top physical boundary:
i = 1:np
j = mp
c23(:,mp)

The artifact would likely appear as a pressure-gradient or vertical-coupling feature aligned with a
physical side boundary, especially near terrain that does not smoothly flatten before the edge.
This is probably harmless for flat topography, cyclic boundaries, or topography that has already been
smoothly tapered to zero normal slope before the physical domain edge. It is a real latent issue for
sloped topography intersecting physical side boundaries.

The safest fix depends on the intended physical meaning of side boundaries.

Option 1: Keep legacy zero-normal-slope terrain behavior, but make it explicit and
smooth
If physical side boundaries are intended to enforce zero-normal terrain slope, then the existing c13=0 /
c23=0 behavior is conceptually consistent with topo.F90.
In that case, add diagnostics and documentation, and require or perform topo tapering before the
boundary.
For example, before topo() overwrites the physical edge values, compute the incoming boundary slope
and warn if it is non-negligible:

  maxslope=maxval(abs(zs(2,1:mp)-zs(1,1:mp)))/dx
  if(maxslope.gt.slope_tol)then
 print*,’WARNING:␣nonzero␣input␣topo␣slope␣at␣left␣physical␣boundary:’, &
 maxslope
  endif
endif

Similarly:

  maxslope=maxval(abs(zs(np,1:mp)-zs(np-1,1:mp)))/dx
  ...
endif

if(botedge.eq.1)then
  maxslope=maxval(abs(zs(1:np,2)-zs(1:np,1)))/dy
  ...
endif

if(topedge.eq.1)then
  maxslope=maxval(abs(zs(1:np,mp)-zs(1:np,mp-1)))/dy
  ...

 95

endif

Then require topography to be padded or tapered so that:

dzs/dx = 0 at left/right physical boundaries
dzs/dy = 0 at bottom/top physical boundaries

This preserves backward compatibility and avoids introducing nonzero terrain metrics through physical
boundaries.

Option 2: Allow sloped terrain at physical boundaries using one-sided metric derivatives
If sloped topography is intended to intersect the physical side boundary, then metric.F90 should not
hard-set the boundary metrics to zero. Instead, compute them with one-sided differences consistent
with go.
For example, define:

q = 1.0_prec/go

Then use centered differences in the interior:

do j=1,mp
  do i=1+leftedge,np-rightedge
    c13(i,j)=0.5_prec*(q(i+1,j)-q(i-1,j))*go(i,j)/dx
  enddo
enddo

and one-sided second-order differences at physical x boundaries:

  do j=1,mp
    c13(1,j)=(-3.0_prec*q(1,j)+4.0_prec*q(2,j)-q(3,j)) &
      *go(1,j)/(2.0_prec*dx)
  enddo
endif

  do j=1,mp
    c13(np,j)=(3.0_prec*q(np,j)-4.0_prec*q(np-1,j)+q(np-2,j)) &
      *go(np,j)/(2.0_prec*dx)
  enddo
endif

Similarly for c23:

do i=1,np
  do j=1+botedge,mp-topedge
    c23(i,j)=0.5_prec*(q(i,j+1)-q(i,j-1))*go(i,j)/dy
  enddo
enddo

with one-sided physical y-boundary values:

if(botedge.eq.1)then

 96

FIRETEC Bug Resolution Log June 2026

  do i=1,np
    c23(i,1)=(-3.0_prec*q(i,1)+4.0_prec*q(i,2)-q(i,3)) &
      *go(i,1)/(2.0_prec*dy)
  enddo
endif

if(topedge.eq.1)then
  do i=1,np
    c23(i,mp)=(3.0_prec*q(i,mp)-4.0_prec*q(i,mp-1)+q(i,mp-2)) &
      *go(i,mp)/(2.0_prec*dy)
  enddo
endif

This makes the boundary metric a continuation of the local topographic slope rather than a hard zero.
However, this change is not sufficient by itself if topo.F90 still overwrites the physical edge terrain values.
To truly allow nonzero boundary slope, topo.F90 should preserve the physical edge cells and only fill
ghost cells consistently.
For example, instead of:

zs(1,j)=zs(2,j)

use ghost-cell extrapolation such as:

if(leftedge.eq.1) then
  do j=1-ih,mp+ih
 do i=1,ih
      zs(1-i,j)=zs(1,j)+real(i,prec)*(zs(1,j)-zs(2,j))
 enddo
  enddo
endif

and similarly for the other physical sides.

Option 3: Add an explicit gridlist option
A robust compatibility-preserving fix would be to add a gridlist option such as:

integer :: itopobc = 0

with behavior:

itopobc = 0:
  legacy behavior
  force zero-normal-slope topo at physical edges
  force c13/c23 = 0 at physical edges

itopobc = 1:
  preserve physical edge topo
  fill ghost topo by extrapolation
  compute c13/c23 at physical edges using one-sided differences

itopobc = 2:
  legacy behavior, but warn or abort if input topo has nonzero boundary slope

 97

This avoids changing existing results while making the boundary metric behavior intentional and
testable.

Diagnostic test
Recommended tests:

1. Flat topography: c13 and c23 should remain zero everywhere.
2. Linear slope crossing a physical x boundary: legacy behavior should show c13 forced to zero at i=1
 or i=np; one-sided metric behavior should produce a smooth c13 field.
3. Linear slope crossing a physical y boundary: legacy behavior should show c23 forced to zero at j=1
 or j=mp; one-sided metric behavior should produce a smooth c23 field.
4. Real topography with physical side boundaries: compare pressure-gradient artifacts near xmin/xmax
 ,→ /ymin/ymax.
5. Same real topography tapered to zero slope near boundaries: artifacts should be reduced if the
 metric discontinuity is the source.

Useful fields to output and inspect:

If artifacts disappear with flat topography or with smoothly tapered boundary topography, but appear
with sloped terrain intersecting physical boundaries, this metric boundary treatment is a plausible
cause.
